A TLS fingerprint is the pattern of encryption options an app offers when it opens a secure connection, and each app\'s network library has its own. For the first 7 days the app learns which fingerprints every app normally uses, without reading any content. If an app later connects in a way it never has before and was not updated, that can reveal a hidden SDK, a tampered app, or interception.

New TLS fingerprint without an app update. Tap for details.

What changed: %1$s opened an encrypted connection using a TLS fingerprint it has never used on this phone before. The app was not updated, so an update does not explain it.

Possible reasons:
• A hidden SDK or library inside the app started making its own connections.
• Something is impersonating the app, such as a modified copy or code injected into it.
• A tool on this phone is intercepting the app's connections (a proxy, debugging or “security” app).
• Harmless: the app switched to a built-in browser or a different network library.

What to do: If you recently installed a proxy, ad blocker, antivirus or debugging tool, it is the likely cause. Otherwise update the app from the Play Store, check its permissions, and uninstall it if you don\'t trust it. If you recognise the change, tap Trust.
Each app\'s encrypted connections are fingerprinted (JA4, with JA3 for compatibility) from the unencrypted handshake. Nothing is decrypted.

resources.string: Why am I seeing this ad?
Mic and camera timeline, location audit, ad-tracking checklist
What this can and can\'t do

Ads inside Facebook and Instagram come from Meta\'s own servers, the same ones that load your feed. Blocking them would break those apps, so this app doesn\'t try. What it can do: show which apps used your mic or camera, which apps can see your location, block ad SDKs inside other apps, and walk you through the settings that feed ad targeting.
Location: GPS, nearby Wi-Fi networks and your IP address tell ad networks where you are and where you have been.
Same Wi-Fi as friends: people sharing an internet connection share an IP address, so platforms link them and show one person ads based on what another searched.
Website pixels: shops and sites send your visits back to Meta and Google with tracking pixels, even if you never tap an ad.
Searches and accounts: what you search, watch and buy while signed in feeds the same ad profile.

What the mic timeline proves: if no app used the microphone while you talked about something, the ad came from these other signals. It only covers time when protection was on, and Android also shows a green dot whenever the mic or camera is in use.
Recorded while protection is on. Android does not say which app is using the mic or camera, so the app that was on screen when it started is shown as the likely one.
Allow Usage Access so the likely app can be named. Without it, uses are still recorded but shown as “Unknown app”.
